findings.title: Arbitrary File Write (ZipSlip via Symbolic Links)
findings.description: The `unpack.ts` and `write-entry.ts` modules contain logic to prevent symlink traversal, but `ensureNoSymlink` (unpack.ts:679) only checks the path during extraction. If `preservePaths` is true, or if an attacker can manipulate the `cwd` or entry path before sanitation, they can write to arbitrary filesystem locations.
steps_to_exploit: Craft a tarball containing an entry with a symlink that points to a sensitive location outside the target extraction directory.
Include a file entry whose path uses the symlink for resolution.
Extract the archive without sufficient validation to overwrite system files or binaries.
findings.impact: Full system compromise; an attacker can overwrite arbitrary files as the process user.

findings.title: Use of Deprecated and Thread-Unsafe process.umask()
findings.description: The `src/process-umask.ts` and `src/unpack.ts` files rely on `process.umask()`, which is deprecated and dangerous in multi-threaded/async Node.js applications as it globally alters the process umask, affecting unrelated code.
steps_to_exploit: Run multiple extraction operations in parallel.
Observe that the umask state is inconsistent between calls.
Predict or force file permissions to be created with incorrect/insecure umask values.
findings.impact: Files can be created with overly permissive permissions (e.g., world-readable) due to race conditions.

findings.title: Insecure Temporary File Deletion on Windows
findings.description: The `unlinkFile` function in `unpack.ts` (73) uses a rename-then-unlink pattern on Windows to handle non-atomic unlinks. However, if an attacker can predict the random bytes, they could perform a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) attack during the window between rename and unlink.
steps_to_exploit: Monitor for the creation of temporary .DELETE files.
Predict or brute-force the random hex string.
Attempt to place a malicious file in that path before the unlink occurs.
findings.impact: Potential for unauthorized file manipulation or local privilege escalation on Windows.

findings.title: Potential Integer Overflow in Large Numbers Parsing
findings.description: In `large-numbers.ts`, `parse` relies on `Math.pow(256, len - i - 1)` and integer arithmetic. While checked against `Number.isSafeInteger`, precision errors can occur if very large, non-safe integers are passed via malicious headers.
steps_to_exploit: Construct a malformed tar header with large values for metadata fields.
Submit the header to a process parsing the tar entry.
Trigger logic errors or unexpected behavior if the parser misinterprets the size or UID/GID.
findings.impact: Unexpected behavior in file parsing, potential for DoS.

findings.title: Insecure Default File Creation Permissions
findings.description: When creating files, `write-entry.ts` defaults to 0o666 (masked by process umask). If the process umask is configured incorrectly or ignored, files could be created with world-writable bits.
steps_to_exploit: Wait for an extraction operation to run.
Access files created by the operation on the host filesystem.
Read or modify the sensitive content of extracted files.
findings.impact: Unauthorized access to sensitive files extracted from a tarball.

findings.title: Denial of Service via Infinite Recursion in Path Resolution
findings.description: The `filesFilter` function (list.ts:27) recursively calls `mapHas` on `dirname(file)`. If an attacker provides a path designed to maximize recursion depth, they can cause a stack overflow.
steps_to_exploit: Craft a file path with an extremely high number of directory components.
Pass this path into the filter function.
Consume stack space until the engine crashes.

evidence.quote: ret = m !== undefined ? m : mapHas(dirname(file), root)

code_refs.quote: ret = m !== undefined ? m : mapHas(dirname(file), root)

findings.title: Insecure Fallback to utimesSync on Failure
findings.description: In `unpack.ts` (1016), if `futimesSync` fails (perhaps due to file locking), the code catches the error and silently attempts `utimesSync`. If both fail, it may suppress valid errors during archive extraction.
steps_to_exploit: Lock the target file from the outside.
Extract a file from an archive.
Observe that the metadata (mtime) might not be updated, potentially violating system state requirements.
findings.impact: Silenced error conditions that lead to inconsistent filesystem state.

findings.title: Lack of Validation on Extracted User/Group IDs
findings.description: The `unpack.ts` logic for setting UIDs and GIDs (1030) does not validate if the IDs are valid for the local system; it blindly passes them to `chown` after a check against `processUid/Gid`.
steps_to_exploit: Create a tarball with arbitrary UID/GID values.
Run the extraction with elevated privileges.
Attempt to set file ownership to arbitrary system users.
findings.impact: Files could be assigned to incorrect users, potentially breaking security isolation.

findings.title: Potential Path Traversal in @-prefixed paths
findings.description: The logic in `create.ts` (59) allows paths starting with '@' to trigger `list()`. This could be abused if an attacker controls the file list to point to unintended file structures.
steps_to_exploit: Provide a path starting with '@' that resolves to an unintended path via traversal (e.g., @../secret).
Observe the tool reading or packaging the unintended file.
findings.impact: Information disclosure; an attacker could include sensitive local files in a created archive.

findings.title: Unsafe Header Parsing with Global Extended Headers
findings.description: Global extended headers are applied to subsequent entries in `parse.ts`. The implementation (368) merges these into an object. Improperly merged attributes might leak across unrelated entries.
steps_to_exploit: Craft a malformed global header.
Place it before a normal file header in the tarball.
Observe metadata attributes leaking from the global header into the local file.
findings.impact: Metadata leakage between files; security attributes like UID/GID could be incorrectly applied.

findings.title: Use of unsafe `Buffer.allocUnsafe`
findings.description: The `list.ts` file uses `Buffer.allocUnsafe` (62, 67), which may contain stale data from process memory. If this buffer is leaked or returned in error conditions, sensitive data might be exposed.
steps_to_exploit: Trigger an extraction/listing process that performs these operations.
Monitor process memory or force an error that outputs the contents of these buffers.
findings.impact: Information disclosure of process memory remnants.

findings.title: Insufficient Validation of Numeric Header Fields
findings.description: The header parsing logic in `header.ts` (101, 103, 105) uses `decNumber`, which is a thin wrapper that may not fully validate values against expected ranges for certain fields.
steps_to_exploit: Provide extremely large numeric values in the Mode, UID, or GID fields.
Attempt to trigger overflows or unexpected numeric behavior in subsequent filesystem calls.
findings.impact: Possible system errors or unexpected file metadata assignments.

findings.title: Command-Injection-like Logic via Dealiasing
findings.description: The `dealias` function (options.ts:706) iterates over user-provided options. A prototype pollution vulnerability is avoided by creating a new object, but it performs a `delete` on `noChmod` which is a mutation on a potentially insecure input object.
steps_to_exploit: Pass an object with a `noChmod` property.
Observe the side effects on the provided option object.
findings.impact: Minor security risk via object mutation; could lead to logic bypasses in configuration validation.

findings.title: Insecure Default `mode` Fixes
findings.description: The `modeFix` function (mode-fix.ts:1) forces executable bits on directories (20, 23, 26). This might bypass system-level security constraints regarding listable directories.
steps_to_exploit: Extract a directory entry that originally lacked read/search bits.
Observe that the extraction process forces search/list permissions.

findings.title: Incomplete Sanitization of Win32 Path Chars
findings.description: While `winchars.ts` (13) attempts to encode Windows special characters, this is a bypassable mechanism. If an attacker knows how these are encoded, they can craft filenames that resolve to unintended paths.
steps_to_exploit: Craft an entry name that incorporates Windows-encoded sequences.
Extract on a platform where path canonicalization handles these sequences.
Access unintended file locations.
findings.impact: Path manipulation; attackers can potentially target files with special characters in their names.
